name: GPU clusters & orchestration
summary: Thousands of accelerators networked and scheduled to act as one machine for training or serving.

D1.guide: What happens to an orchestra if one player stops? Keep that in mind.
text: One chip isn't enough to teach a big AI, so we connect thousands together, like a huge orchestra that has to play in perfect time.
A conductor program decides which chips work on what, and restarts the music if a player stops.
D1.analogy: An enormous orchestra with a conductor.

text: Training a large model splits the work across many accelerators: each holds part of the data, part of the model, or both (data, tensor and pipeline parallelism).
The accelerators exchange results constantly, so fast networking between them is essential.
Schedulers such as Slurm or Kubernetes assign jobs to machines, and training jobs save checkpoints so a hardware failure doesn't lose weeks of work.
D2.analogy: An orchestra with a conductor keeping everyone in time.
D2.analogyBreaks: An orchestra survives a missed note. A synchronised training step waits for the slowest chip, so one failing machine can stall thousands.

predict.question: Why do large training jobs save checkpoints regularly?
options: With thousands of machines failures are routine, and restarting from scratch would waste time
predict.explanation: At large scale some hardware fails often; checkpoints let the job resume from recent progress.

text: Open problems: keeping utilisation high on ever-larger clusters, training across multiple data centres, and scheduling training and inference workloads on shared hardware.
